lead.headline: Israel Votes, and Exit Polls Show No Clear Winner
lead.deck: A majority needs 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats, and exit polls suggest nobody is there yet.
body: Israel held a national election on 27 October to choose its parliament, the Knesset. The Knesset has 120 seats, so a party or group of parties needs 61 to hold a majority. That number is the key to the whole story: with 61, a government can pass laws; without it, it cannot.

Exit polls, which ask voters as they leave polling stations, suggest the result is not clear. CNN reported that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, appear short of outright victory. Channel 12's exit poll projected the prime minister's bloc falling from 68 seats in the previous Knesset to 50 seats. Turnout, the share of people who voted, was reportedly the highest since at least 1999.

Exit polls are estimates, not results. Official results come from Israel's Central Elections Committee, and the numbers can move as real votes are counted. So the main facts are still to come: the final seat totals, and which parties can join together to reach 61.

Channel 12 gave Netanyahu's bloc 50 seats and Eisenkot's bloc 52, while Channel 13 and Kan put both blocs level at 51. Do the sums with Channel 12: 50 plus 52 is 102, so 18 seats sit outside both blocs. The Jerusalem Post reported that Arab parties were projected at 17 to 18 seats, and NBC News reported that Eisenkot has all but ruled out governing with them. That is why neither man has an easy path to 61.

Turnout was 77.7%, the highest since 1999, according to the Central Elections Committee, with some 5.7 million people voting. Netanyahu's Likud was projected to be the largest single party, at close to 27 seats. Now likely weeks of talks begin, and President Isaac Herzog will ask a candidate to try to form a government.
lead.why: A seat count of 61 decides who can govern, which is why one number can matter more than the total of votes.

world.headline: Ukraine, Russia and the US Plan Three-Way Talks
world.deck: Zelenskyy says they agreed to meet next month; Moscow says fighting will go on.
body: Ukraine's President, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on 26 October that Ukraine, Russia and the United States have agreed to hold talks next month. These are called trilateral talks because there are three sides. The Kremlin has since said Russia agreed in principle to meet on 10 November in Abu Dhabi, at the level of negotiating teams rather than presidents.

The two warring sides want different things. Zelenskyy has renewed his call for a meeting with Putin on territorial issues, meaning who controls which land. Putin said talks should aim for lasting security through final agreements, not a short-lived ceasefire, and Russia says it has no intention of halting hostilities while the talks run.
Geography explains why the land question is so hard: the war is being fought over territory, so any deal must say where lines are drawn.

Getting here took shuttle diplomacy. The US envoy Steve Witkoff met Zelenskyy in Oslo on 20 October and Putin in St Petersburg the next day, after which both sides said they were ready to resume talks. The last US-mediated talks were in February, before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.

The gap between the two positions is wide. Russia demands that Ukraine pull out of the part of the eastern Donetsk region it still controls; Ukraine calls that a capitulation. Zelenskyy says any deal needs strong security guarantees and 10 years of funding for Ukraine's army.

One small step has already happened. On 27 October a local ceasefire began around the occupied city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid can get in, although no one has said who will check that it holds.

india.headline: A Warm Bay Sends Cyclone Arnab Toward the Andhra Coast
india.deck: Landfall is forecast in the small hours of 28 October.
body: Geography helps explain why India's east coast is so often in the path of storms. Al Jazeera notes that the Bay of Bengal is a major breeding ground for tropical cyclones. Arnab grew there and is now classed as a very severe cyclonic storm.

Look at the forecast as a map. The weather office expects the centre to come ashore close to Visakhapatnam, between 2 am and 4 am on 28 October. Odisha, further north along the coast, should feel weaker winds of 60 to 80 km/h, while Andhra Pradesh could see 125 to 135 km/h, with gusts up to 150. More than 12 million people live along the projected path.

Preparation is under way on both sides of the state border: over 84,000 people moved in Andhra Pradesh and over 30,000 in Odisha, about 4,000 shelters are open, and 16 of Odisha's 30 districts closed schools.

Track the storm on the map. When Al Jazeera reported, Arnab was 260 km southeast of Visakhapatnam and forecast to turn northwest, which is why the warnings reach from Andhra Pradesh up into southern Odisha. Odisha's officials planned to move about 48,000 people in all.

The numbers behind the shelters tell their own story. Andhra Pradesh set up 2,131 shelters in its coastal districts, deployed 1,087 medical teams and 1,274 ambulances, readied 8,281 emergency beds and moved 1,351 pregnant women to hospitals before the storm arrived. More than 30,000 fishing boats were secured along the coast, according to the Associated Press.

Travel stopped too. At least 21 flights were cancelled at Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam on Tuesday, and at least 50 trains were cancelled. Andhra Pradesh's Chief Minister, N. Chandrababu Naidu, said there is no need for people to panic, but they have to take precautions.

The forecast also explains the evacuation map. The strongest winds are expected where the centre crosses the Andhra Pradesh coast, which is where most people moved: more than 84,000 there, compared with more than 30,000 in Odisha. By Tuesday, heavy rain and gusty winds had already started lashing parts of the Andhra Pradesh coast, according to the Associated Press.
india.why: Where a coast faces warm sea water, shelters and early warnings decide how many people are safe.

us.headline: The Fed Decides on Interest Rates as Traders Expect a Hold
us.deck: Traders put about an 11% chance on a hike this week.
body: The Federal Reserve is the United States' central bank. Its two-day policy meeting began on Tuesday 27 October, and its decision is due on Wednesday 28 October at 2 pm US Eastern time. The interest rate it sets influences how much it costs to borrow money.

According to Reuters, traders put about an 11% chance on a rate hike this week and about 82% on a hike by December. In other words, most traders expect no change now, but many expect a rise later in the year.
Interest rates matter beyond the United States. A stronger dollar was one reason the Indian rupee slipped past 95 per dollar in early trade on Tuesday, according to DT Next.

The Fed's target range now stands at 3.75% to 4.00%. A CNBC survey of 30 economists and strategists found 93% expect a pause this week and 76% expect a hike in December. The chair, Kevin Warsh, has repeatedly declined to tell markets what he plans to do before the committee meets, which adds some uncertainty.

What does the rate change in a family's budget? Most US credit cards carry variable rates that move closely with the Fed's, and the average rate on a new card offer is 23.96%, according to LendingTree. Mortgages follow longer-term borrowing costs instead: with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%, the average 30-year fixed mortgage is close to 7.4%, according to Mortgage News Daily.

Higher rates have winners too. Because the Fed has kept rates high, savers earn relatively attractive interest on high-yield savings accounts. If the Fed holds this week, credit card rates are likely to stay near today's levels, CNBC said.
Traders on Kalshi, a prediction market, put the chance of a hold this week at 93%.

science_and_technology.headline: A Maths Search Turns Up a Possible Dwarf Planet
science_and_technology.deck: 2026 ED138 sits about 46 au from the Sun and is roughly 1,000 km wide.
body: Space distances need their own unit. One astronomical unit (au) is the average distance from Earth to the Sun. A possible dwarf planet found with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, provisionally called 2026 ED138, is about 46 au out. Pluto, for comparison, averages 40 au.
Its width is not yet pinned down: the estimate runs from 600 to 1,500 km, and Mario Juric, who leads Rubin's solar system team, puts it at about 1,000 km.

The key was a program, not a lens. Matthew Holman and Kevin Napier wrote search code that links billions of moving-object detections that belong to the same object. Holman ran Rubin data through it on 13 October. Confirmation would make 2026 ED138 the sixth dwarf planet after Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

Finding it once was not enough. Mario Juric of the University of Washington, who leads Rubin's solar system team, confirmed the object with 20 more observations going back to March 2026, and the team traced more than ten years of its orbit in archival images dating to 2016. The Minor Planet Center of the International Astronomical Union announced the discovery, and Juric and Holman, of the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, presented it at a planetary science meeting in Spokane.
Why did nobody spot it before? It sits in a star-crowded part of the sky, which hid it for years.

Being big is not enough to count as a dwarf planet. Further observations are needed to tell whether 2026 ED138 has enough mass for its own gravity to pull it into a round shape, which is a key requirement.

Rubin is only getting started. Its sky survey, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, began in June 2026, and in April the team announced over 11,000 new asteroids, including roughly 380 new objects beyond Neptune.
If it is confirmed, the Rubin team says 2026 ED138 would be among the largest dwarf planets ever discovered in this region of the solar system.
science_and_technology.why: Mathematics and software let astronomers find a world that no one had spotted in decades of looking.

economics.headline: India's Rupee Slips Past 95 per Dollar as Oil Stays Near $115
economics.deck: The currency was about 95.22 in early trade on Tuesday.
body: An exchange rate tells you how much of one currency buys another. On Tuesday 27 October the rupee fell 7 paise to 95.22 against the US dollar in early trade, according to DT Next, weighed down by high oil prices and a stronger dollar. HDFC Sky reported a provisional close of 95.12.

India buys oil from abroad, and oil is priced in dollars, so a weaker rupee makes the same barrel cost more. On Monday a barrel of Brent crude settled at $115.81, per FinanceFeeds. India imports nearly 90% of the crude oil it needs, Business Standard reports, and since 12 October the Reserve Bank has supplied all the daily dollars that the state oil firms Indian Oil, HPCL and BPCL need through a special window.
The Reserve Bank of India raised its repo rate to 5.5% on 7 October, according to BBN Times.

Small moves add up. The rupee settled at 95.15 on Monday, its third straight day of decline, losing 77 paise over three sessions. Forex traders said it recovered a little on likely support from the Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank, but could not hold out against money leaving the country.

That outflow is easy to measure. Foreign institutional investors sold Indian shares worth Rs 1,462.49 crore, in net terms, on Monday, according to DT Next. When foreign investors sell shares and take money home, they swap rupees for dollars, and more rupees for sale pushes the rupee's price down.

Oil adds pressure from the other side. Analysts linked higher crude to Houthi attacks on Saudi oil sites, and flows of crude through the Hormuz region fell to about 8.5 million barrels a day in the week to 19 October, down from more than 20 million the week before, according to Kpler. India must buy dollars to pay for that oil, which raises demand for dollars even more.

What next? Anuj Choudhary of Mirae Asset Sharekhan expects the rupee to trade with a negative bias, between 94.85 and 95.50 per dollar. Business Recorder reported that higher oil prices and outflows have left the rupee relying on the central bank's support.
The dollar itself was a little stronger: the dollar index, which compares it with other major currencies, rose 0.06% to 101.86.
economics.why: Prices for oil are set in dollars, so currency moves reach petrol pumps and shops.

explainer.title: Why 61 of 120 matters
body: In a parliament, a majority means more than half the seats. Israel's Knesset has 120 seats, so 61 is a majority.

When no party reaches 61 alone, parties must join together to form a government. This is called a coalition. The parties bargain over who gets which job and which policies come first, and that can take time.

lead.headline: Israel Votes, With No Clear Winner
body: Israel held an election on 27 October. Its parliament has 120 seats. A majority needs 61 seats.
Exit polls suggest nobody won a clear victory. Exit polls ask people as they leave the polling place.
Exit polls are only estimates. Official results will come later from the election officials, and the count can change. A party or group needs 61 seats to have a majority and to form a government.
